Wit
wit
n. and v. (knowledge, understanding; in the archaic idiom to wit, namely; rendering Hebrew yada, Greek in explanatory apposition)
Old English witan, to know — the same root as German wissen and English wise. In the KJV wit almost never means humour; it means knowledge, and its commonest use is the connective to wit, meaning namely.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Wit in the Authorized Version is knowledge, and it is one of the archaisms most likely to trip a modern reader. Its dominant use is the connective phrase to wit, meaning namely or that is to say, and it introduces some of the New Testament's weightiest clauses. Paul defines reconciliation with it: “To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:19). He defines the object of the creation's groaning with it: believers groan within themselves, “waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23) — a clause that fixes Christian hope on a bodily and not a merely spiritual future. As a verb of knowing it appears in the narratives: Abraham's servant “held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not” (Genesis 24:21), watching in silence to learn the answer; and Miriam “stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him” (Exodus 2:4), a girl waiting beside a river to find out whether her brother would live. And the Psalter gives the idiom the modern ear knows best, of sailors in a storm: “They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end” (Psalm 107:27) — the end of knowing, where the next verse has them cry unto the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Knowledge, not humour. To wit means namely, and it introduces the definition of reconciliation and of the adoption we await; as a verb it is the silent watching of Abraham's servant and of Miriam; wits' end is where sailors begin to pray.

WIT, v.t. or i. [Sax. witan, to know.] To know; obsolete except in the phrase, to wit, that is, to know, namely, videlicet.

2. WIT, n. Primarily, the intellect; the understanding or mental powers.

3. The association of ideas in a manner natural and pleasing, but unexpected.

4. A man of genius; as, the wits of the age.

5. Wits, in the plural, soundness of mind; intellect; as, at his wits' end. Ps. 107.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 5:19 — "To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation."

Romans 8:23 — "And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body."

Genesis 24:21 — "And the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not."

Psalm 107:27 — "They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end."

Modern Corruption

The archaism is simply lost on modern readers, who hear wit as cleverness or humour and so skip past the connective that introduces some of Scripture's most compact doctrinal statements.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the problem is linguistic drift, and it costs the reader something specific. To wit is an apposition marker: what follows is not an addition but a definition of what preceded. Miss it in 2 Corinthians 5:19 and the verse becomes a general statement about reconciliation; catch it and the verse is defining the ministry Paul has just described, and doing so in the most precise language available — God was in Christ, reconciling, not imputing their trespasses. That last clause is the negative side of imputation, and it is joined to the positive in the following verse: He was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him. The whole doctrine of the great exchange stands in a sentence introduced by an archaism most readers slide over.

Romans 8:23 rewards the same attention and corrects a common error. Christians frequently speak of the believer's hope as escape from the body, and much popular piety is functionally Platonic — the soul released, the body left behind, heaven as disembodiment. Paul says the thing waited for is the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body. The apposition rules out any reading in which the body is dispensable; the creation itself groans for the same deliverance, and the resurrection of the flesh is in every catholic creed. Recovering the small connective recovers the doctrine: what a Christian awaits is not a better afterlife but a raised body in a renewed world, and the vocabulary of Scripture is careful about it even where its English has gone quiet.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English witan, to know, cognate with Latin videre and Greek oida; the phrase to wit renders Hebrew lada'ath (to know) and Greek appositional constructions, and corresponds to the Latin videlicet.

expand to see more

Old English witan — to know; the root of wit, wise, wisdom, and the archaic wist (knew) and wot (knows).

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; the verb rendered to wit in Genesis 24:21 and Exodus 2:4.

Greek hos hoti — the appositional construction in 2 Corinthians 5:19 that the KJV renders to wit.

Latin videlicet — namely, to wit; the legal Latin equivalent, abbreviated viz.

Greek apolytrosis (G629) — redemption, a buying back; the noun the apposition defines in Romans 8:23.

Usage

"“To wit, that God was in Christ” — not an addition but a definition of the reconciliation just named."

"“The adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body” — the apposition that rules out a disembodied hope."

"“At their wits' end” — the end of knowing, and the verse before men cry unto the LORD."
